advisor.summary: Qualified improvement property — an improvement the taxpayer makes to the interior of nonresidential real property after the building first goes into service — is 15-year MACRS property under §168(e)(6), which places it inside the 20-year window for 100% bonus depreciation under §168(k). The practical effect is dramatic: a tenant buildout or interior renovation that would naively land on a 39-year schedule instead deducts in full in the placed-in-service year, and the classification is categorical — no engineering study required. The statutory exclusions are just as categorical: building enlargements, elevators and escalators, and internal structural framework never qualify, and residential interiors are out entirely. Prior-year misclassifications are repaired prospectively through an automatic method change with a §481(a) catch-up in the tradition of Rev. Proc. 2020-25. The engine models the QIP amount as a current entity-level deduction.
mechanics: The §168(e)(6) definition runs on three gates: an interior portion of nonresidential real property, an improvement placed in service after the building itself first was, and work done by the taxpayer — with statutory carve-outs for enlargement, elevators and escalators, and internal structural framework.

With a 15-year recovery period, QIP is qualified property under §168(k): 100% bonus in the placed-in-service year, made permanent by P.L. 119-21 for property that is both acquired after January 19, 2025 and placed in service after that date — both legs of the test must be met.

Typical qualifying scope — drywall, interior doors and ceilings, interior lighting, flooring, interior plumbing and electrical distribution, fire suppression — comes off invoices, not engineering studies; the discipline lies in scoping contracts so qualifying and non-qualifying work are separately stated.
A prior-year misclassification (QIP depreciated over 39 years) is corrected through a Form 3115 automatic method change with a §481(a) catch-up, on the template of Rev. Proc. 2020-25.
Where the year-one loss would be trapped, electing out of bonus for the 15-year class under §168(k)(7) leaves QIP on 15-year straight line — still far faster than the 39-year default.

requirements: A nonresidential building already in service before the improvements — the day-one buildout of a brand-new building is not QIP.
Interior improvements only, made by the taxpayer; enlargements, elevators/escalators, and structural framework are excluded by statute.
Invoices and contracts scoped so qualifying interior work is stated separately from excluded work.
A use path for the deduction — passive-loss gating on the rental side, the excess-business-loss limit on the business side.
risks: The leading audit theory is misclassification — sweeping structural, exterior, or enlargement work into QIP — and the exam is won or lost on invoices, not doctrine; no signature case exists because the definition is mechanical.

A large year-one deduction can be trapped by §469 for landlords without REPS or short-term-rental treatment, or limited by §461(l) on the business side — run the elect-out analysis before defaulting to bonus.
Fully bonused improvements carry recapture exposure on disposition.
Who deducts turns on who owns the improvements — lease terms and construction-allowance treatment decide landlord versus tenant, and getting the lease wrong forfeits the deduction.
State bonus decoupling puts the state deduction on a far slower schedule.
stateNotes: Conformity: even states that decouple from §168(k) generally respect the 15-year life, so QIP recovers at 15-year straight line for state purposes in addback states — a split-schedule computation built once and reused.
Missouri conforms to federal bonus through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121), so the full year-one deduction flows straight to the Missouri return.
PTET interaction: the deduction reduces the electing entity’s income before any PTET computation; re-project the PTET accrual once the QIP decision is made.
reviewChecklist: Building confirmed nonresidential and in service before the improvement.
Invoices scoped: qualifying interior work separately stated; enlargements, elevators, and structural framing excluded.
Bonus versus §168(k)(7) elect-out analysis completed against the client’s loss-usability picture.
Ownership of the improvements (landlord versus tenant) confirmed against the lease.
Prior-year 39-year misclassifications screened; Form 3115 catch-up prepared where found.

client.teaser: Interior upgrades to commercial space can be written off in one year, not spread over 39.
client.headline: Deduct interior building work now, not over 39 years
plainEnglish: Improve the inside of a commercial building — remodel offices, build out tenant space, upgrade lighting or flooring — and the default tax schedule spreads your deduction over 39 years. At that pace, today's project is still dripping onto your return decades from now.

The tax law puts most interior work on commercial buildings in a fast lane instead. It can be written off in full in the year the work is done. No engineering study is needed — the category itself qualifies.

The main rules: interior work only, on a commercial building already in use. Additions, elevators, and structural framing do not count. We scope the project with your contractor up front so the invoices tell the right story, and we check that a big deduction actually helps you this year.
client.analogy: It is like finding an express lane for a payment the law planned to mail you in pieces over 39 years.
benefits: Deduct 100% of qualifying interior improvements in year one
Covers tenant buildouts, remodels, lighting, and flooring
A slower schedule can be chosen when the big deduction would go to waste
steps: WE review the renovation plans against the qualification rules before work begins.
WE coordinate with your contractor so bids keep qualifying work separate.
WE model the full write-off against a slower schedule and file the right election.
YOU send us the construction contracts and invoices as the project wraps up.
clientCommitments: Bring us in at the planning stage, before contracts are signed
Have contractors itemize invoices between interior work and excluded work
